title: Stack operational semantics
prompt_markdown: What fundamental data ordering principle governs a `stack` data structure?
hints: Think of plates stacked on a table.

content.explanation: A stack operates on LIFO (Last-In First-Out) semantics: the element most recently pushed onto the stack is the first element popped off.

title: Amortized complexity of monotonic stack algorithm
prompt_markdown: What is the total time complexity of running a monotonic stack algorithm across an array of length $N$?
hints: How many times can each individual element be pushed and popped?

content.explanation: Even though a while loop is nested inside a for loop, every single index is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped at most once across the entire algorithm execution. Total operations: at most 2N = O(N).

title: RPN operand ordering
prompt_markdown: When evaluating Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), if stack contains `[10, 2]` and operator `-` is encountered, what is the correct calculation?
hints: The first popped value is the second operand.

content.explanation: In RPN evaluation, popping yields `b = 2` (right operand) and `a = 10` (left operand). The expression is `a - b`, which is `10 - 2 = 8`.

title: Predict monotonic stack contents during Daily Temperatures
prompt_markdown: Given temperatures `[73, 74, 71, 69, 72]`, trace the state of the monotonic stack (storing indices) after processing each temperature index 0 through 4.
hints: Stack stores indices. While current temp > stack top temp, pop and record distance.

content.reference_answer:
State Trace of Stack (storing indices):
- i=0 (73): `stack = [0]`
- i=1 (74): 74 > temp[0] (73) -> pop 0, wait time = 1. `stack = [1]`
- i=2 (71): 71 < temp[1] (74) -> push 2. `stack = [1, 2]`
- i=3 (69): 69 < temp[2] (71) -> push 3. `stack = [1, 2, 3]`
- i=4 (72):
  - 72 > temp[3] (69) -> pop 3, wait time for day 3 = 4 - 3 = 1
  - 72 > temp[2] (71) -> pop 2, wait time for day 2 = 4 - 2 = 2
  - 72 < temp[1] (74) -> stop popping. Push 4.
  - Final `stack = [1, 4]`

title: Explain monotonic stack amortized complexity in interviews
prompt_markdown: In an interview, you write a monotonic stack solution containing a `while` loop nested inside a `for` loop. The interviewer asks: 'Doesn't that nested loop make your solution quadratic $O(n^2)$?' How do you rigorously prove to them that it runs in linear $O(n)$ time?
hints: Use aggregate amortized analysis counting push and pop operations per item.

rubric: Rebuts the naive assumption that nested loops automatically imply O(n^2)
Uses aggregate analysis: each element in the input is pushed onto the stack exactly once
Explains that an element can be popped from the stack at most once in its entire lifetime
Proves that total inner while loop iterations across the entire algorithm are bounded by N, giving O(N) total time
content.reference_answer:
1. Why Nested Loops Do Not Mean Quadratic:
A nested loop is only quadratic if the inner loop performs $O(n)$ work for *every* iteration of the outer loop. In a monotonic stack, work is not independent across iterations.

2. The Aggregate Amortized Proof:
- Consider the lifecycle of any individual index $i$ in the array:
  - Element $i$ is pushed onto the stack exactly once (in the outer for-loop).
  - Element $i$ can be popped from the stack at most once (inside the inner while-loop). Once popped, it is gone forever and cannot be re-examined.
- Therefore, across the entire execution of the program over an array of size $N$:
  $$\text{Total Pushes} = N$$
  $$\text{Total Pops} \le N$$
- The body of the inner `while` loop executes only when an element is popped. Since at most $N$ pops can ever occur, the inner loop body executes at most $N$ times *in total across all outer loop iterations combined*.

Conclusion: Total operations = $N \text{ pushes} + N \text{ pops} = 2N = O(N)$ linear time.
